paper_title: Which Agent's Skill Should Change? Group-Relative Credit Assignment for Evolving Multi-Agent Teams

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Cooperative language-model agents can improve without weight updates by revising reusable skills, but only if a shared team reward is traced to the responsible agent and skill. Existing methods credit the skills present in each trajectory, yet presence is not responsibility: a harmful skill active in successful runs still earns positive credit. We present \textbf{GRSE}, \textbf{G}roup-\textbf{R}elative \textbf{S}kill \textbf{E}volution, which assigns behavioral credit by comparison: inspired by GRPO, it executes each question several times under the same skill libraries and contrasts the executions to credit agent--skill pairs, with structured diagnosis of failures. On HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors, GRSE outperforms MASkills, the closest prior method, on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except open-domain, with the largest gains on multi-hop questions ($+6.7$ and $+3.2$ F1). Its gains rest on better-grounded retrieval rather than answers given without evidence, and its learned skills transfer between the multi-hop tasks. GRSE is robust to corrupted libraries: starting from planted harmful skills, it credits every planted skill with the correct sign and recovers the score of a clean library ($+6.3$ points), whereas MASkills misattributes two and falls below its starting point.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Language-model agents increasingly work in teams: one agent collects evidence, another reasons over it, and the team is judged by single outcome (Cemri et al., 2026; Ghareeb et al., 2026; Tran et al., 2025; Dang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Xia et al., 2026b; Hong et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023). Improving such team requires answering credit assignment question: which agents behavior, and which step of it, produced success or *Corresponding addresses: authors {ma.yanan;banerjee.imon}@mayo.com. Our code is available at https://github.com/yananma1029/GRSE-Skills. email failure? The question is classical in multi-agent reinforcement learning, where shared reward is decomposed with difference rewards or counterfactual baselines (Wolpert and Tumer, 2001; Foerster et al., 2018; Rashid et al., 2020), and it has recently been posed for language-model teams as automated failure attribution (Zhang et al., 2025). wrong answer may stem from evidence collection, an incomplete handoff, or downstream reasoning (Wang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025), and the agent whose output is wrong is often not the agent whose behavior needs to change. For example, reasoner answers wrongly when the retriever misses the evidence. We study this problem in setting where model parameters stay fixed and each agents behavior is specified by natural-language skills, reusable procedures that the agent reads and follows (Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023; Alzubi et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026). Skills make behavior editable, so credit becomes actionable: once responsibility is located, the responsible procedure can be revised. Existing experienceand skill-learning methods, however, assign credit coarsely, which often distill lessons from whole trajectories, and mainly focus on single-agent setting (Shinn et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2026; Ouyang et al., 2026). Meanwhile MASkill, the recent two-agent SOTA, credits each skill from single trajectory in isolation (Yao et al., 2026). However, without contrast, skill that is present in every execution also receives credit for the successes it did not cause: in our robustness study, MASkills raises the utility of planted harmful skill over three iterations, whereas our method labels it harmful and prunes it (Appendix C). Comparison between executions already guide experience distillation, skill refinement, and prompt optimization (Cai et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Zehle, 2026), but they have not been used to localize teams outcome to individual agents behaviors. Behavioral credit assignment in agent teams poses two challenges. The example is from one training run on LoCoMo single-hop questions, in which Agent 1 retrieves evidence and Agent 2 answers. In iteration 1, failure that surfaces in Agent 2s answer is traced to Agent 1s retrieval, and new retrieval skill is induced. In iteration 3, this skill is credited as harmful in the shown group but helpful across the iterations 16 groups, so it is refined rather than pruned. In Figure 1, Agent 2 answers not mentioned in three of four executions of the same question, yet Agent 2 behaves correctly given its input. The decisive difference lies in Agent 1s search query, which retrieves the answer only in the successful execution. Second, an attribution must be specific and checkable before it can drive revision. defective procedure, missing capability, and tool failure call for different responses, and an explanation that cites no execution step cannot be verified. Across questions, attributions must also be aggregated without counting repeated executions of one question as independent evidence. We introduce GRSE, Group-Relative Skill Evolution, training-free framework that evolves cooperative agents skills through group relative behavioral credit assignment. Following GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), GRSE samples multiple complete team rollouts of the same question under fixed skill libraries and compute relative within-group advantages (3.1). group-relative critic compares agent behavior and handoffs across these rollouts to assign feedback to individual agentskill pairs. structured diagnosis grounds each attribution in failure type, cited failed and successful steps, and an edit action, and reference checks reject attributions that the executions do not support (3.2). The accepted attributions are aggregated across questions (3.3) and applied as skill updates through the editing operators and validation gate of MASkills (3.4). Figure 1 shows both levels of attribution within single run: across agents, responsibility shifts from the answering agent to the retrieving agent; within an agent, previously learned skill is later credited as harmful and diagnosed as skill defect. Our contributions are threefold: We formulate skill evolution for cooperative agents as behavioral credit assignment: with model parameters fixed and skills as editable units, shared team outcome must be attributed to the agent and skills responsible for it. We address this by jointly comparing same-question team executions, which produces agentskill feedback while preserving the handoffs needed to interpret each agents behavior and the proposed revision. 2 We make these attributions verifiable and actionable: structured failure analysis links each attribution to failure type, checked step references, and an edit action, and cross-question aggregation weighs attributions by the number of distinct questions that support them. We evaluate GRSE on HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors. GRSE outperforms MASkills on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except open-domain. Its credit identifies and removes harmful skills that MASkills retains. Answer-transition and learned-skill analyses show that GRSEs gains come from fewer broken answers and better-grounded retrieval.

sections.title: 2.1 Reflection and Experience Memory
sections.content: Experience-based adaptation stores information from past interactions to guide future decisions. Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) records verbal reflections for subsequent attempts. ExpeL (Zhao et al., 2024) extracts reusable insights from successes and failures, including comparisons on the same task. AMEM (Xu et al., 2026) constructs linked notes and updates their contextual attributes as new memories arrive. ReasoningBank (Ouyang et al., 2026) distills reasoning strategies, and its memory-aware testtime scaling uses multiple executions to enrich memory curation. These methods actively transform experience rather than simply retaining raw traces. Memory and skills also interact: MemSkill (Zhang et al., 2026b) learns to select memory-management skills and revises its skill bank, while MSCE (Tang et al., 2026) promotes evidence-supported procedural policies into skills and maintains them using feedback. These methods decide what experience to keep and how to organize it, whereas GRSE instead decides where execution evidence should act, assigning it to editable skills owned by individual agents.

sections.title: 2.2 Reusable Skill Discovery and Evolution
sections.content: Skill libraries turn experience into procedures that can be invoked and revised. Voyager (Wang et al., 2023) maintains executable code skills, and EvoSkill (Alzubi et al., 2026) uses an executor, proposer, and skill builder to discover and refine skills from task feedback. SkillRL (Xia et al., 2026a) distills failed trajectories into lessons, organizes skills into general and task-specific categories, and evolves the library alongside reinforcement learning of the agent policy. These methods learn skills for single executing agent, so they never have to decide which agents skill to revise. MASkills (Yao et al., 2026) extends skill learning to cooperative teams through skill-conditioned credit, hierarchical aggregation, and skill editing, but it credits each trajectory on its own. We retain its skill representation and editing operators and change how credit is formed: GRSE jointly compares same-question team executions, and structured diagnosis links each failure to an agentskill target, cited execution steps, and checked edit action.

sections.title: 2.3 Group-Relative and Contrastive Feedback
sections.content: GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) uses within-question rewards to optimize model parameters. Training-Free GRPO (Cai et al., 2025) instead distills semantic feedback from rollout groups into experiential context. Several methods already apply comparisons to skills: SkillCAT (Chen et al., 2026) contrasts same-task success/failure pairs, evaluates patches through replay, and organizes skills for routing. SkillCome (Li et al., 2026) combines within-group contrast with memories of failure and contrast patterns. CANTANTE (Zehle, 2026) contrasts joint prompt configurations on the same query to provide per-agent optimization signals. In these methods, the contrast either compares outcomes or varies the configuration being optimized. GRSE holds the skills fixed and contrasts the teams behavior across executions, so that an outcome difference can be traced to an agent, skill, and cited step.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: GRSE attributes teams outcome to the behaviors of individual agents and turns these attributions into revisions of the responsible behavior. Each agents behavior is specified by skill library, while language-model parameters and agent roles stay fixed. Every iteration has three main steps (Figure 1): grouped rollouts provide contrasting executions of the same question (3.1); group-relative critic assigns behavioral credit to agentskill pairs and grounds it in structured failure analysis (3.2); and the attributions are aggregated across questions (3.3) and applied as validated skill updates (3.4). Algorithm 1 summarizes the update loop.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We follow the setting of MASkills (Yao et al., 2026), the closest prior SOTA for multi-agent skill evolution. Each method consists of two agents with task-specific roles that communicate sequentially, and the second agent produces the final answer. The agents are executed by one of two open-weight actors, Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) and Gemma-4-31B-it (Gemma Team, 2026), each conditioned on its own skill library. We use these two recent released open-weight model of similar size from different families to test whether credit assignment depends on the actor. fixed Qwen3.827B model serves as critic and skill optimizer for all methods. Model parameters and agent roles stay fixed. The agents change only through their skills, which are revised according to the assigned credit. All skill-evolution methods start from empty libraries and run for five iterations. GRSE samples four team trajectories per question, whereas MASkills samples one. Final libraries are evaluated with temperature-zero decoding. Detailed model, data and optimization settings appear in Appendix A.

sections.title: 4.2 Benchmarks
sections.content: Datasets and metrics. We evaluate on HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) for multi-hop question answering and LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) for long-memory conversational reasoning. We use the distractorhard subset and report the answer-token F1 for HotpotQA. LoCoMo covers multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, and single-hop questions. We report the category-specific F1 and smoothed BLEU. Baselines. We group baselines by whether they use the agent team. Single-model baselines answer with one model and no agents or skills. On HotpotQA, we run four prompting methods with the same actor, questions, passages, answer-format instruction, and metric as the agent teams, including IO (direct answer), Chain-of-Thought(CoT; (Wei et al., 2022)), CoT with self-consistency (CoTSC; (Wang et al., 2022); majority vote over five samples), and Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) (at most three feedback-and-revision rounds). On LoCoMo, the full-context baseline follows the benchmark protocol (Maharana et al., 2024) with the actor model reads the entire conversation and answers directly. Two-agent baselines share the team, roles, and actor with GRSE. The empty-library team is this team before any skill is learned (iteration 0). For HotpotQA, all teams follow the agent prompts and short-answer instructions from the MASkills implementation, with questions and distractor passages supplied by the dataset. For LoCoMo, agent teams use categoryspecific task prompts. All the prompts are detailed in Appendix F. We report each two-agent method as the mean over three training runs, because the learned libraries vary with the sampled rollouts and the critics outputs, whereas single-model baselines have no training stage and are evaluated once. GRSE variants. We report GRSE and GRSE w/o structure analysis, which retains group-relative feedback but omits the prescribed failure-diagnosis schema and its checks, in main analysis. We report GRSE w/o structure and the other three variants in ablation studies: GRSE w/ label retains structured diagnosis and additionally uses dataset labels to condition the critic and organize update evidence; GRSE with 𝐺=1 samples one trajectory per question; and DAPO filter keeps four rollouts but, following the dynamic sampling of DAPO (Yu et al., 2025), sends only groups whose rewards differ to the critic.

sections.title: 5.5 Ablation studies
sections.content: To isolate the contributions of structured diagnosis and group sampling, we learn one skill library shared by all four LoCoMo categories (Qwen3.8 actor, one run per setting, 842 test questions). We test four ablation settings: GRSE w/o structure; GRSE with 𝐺=1; GRSE with the DAPO filter; and GRSE w/ label (details see Appendix D). From Table 10 we observe that: Both components help. Group contrast gives the critic basis for attribution, and structured analysis checks it. GRSE has the best category average in F1 (54.9) and BLEU (42.2), +2.9 F1 over the empty library, with the largest gains on temporal and open-domain questions. Removing structured diagnosis or group sampling (𝐺=1) lowers the average F1 by 1.0 and 0.8 respectively. Equal-reward groups still inform the critic. The DAPO filter discards the 713 of 32 groups per iteration in which all four rollouts receive the same reward. This lowers the category average by 0.5 F1 and 0.6 BLEU, mostly through open-domain questions (4.1 F1), while single-hop questions gain (+2.4 F1). Even without contrast, equal9 Labels favor the majority category. GRSE w/ label tops the pooled result (All) only through single-hop questions, 54% of the test set (+4.7 F1 and BLEU). It trails GRSE on every other category, most on open-domain (6.7 F1), and has the lowest category average of all variants (53.0 F1). Label-conditioned evidence thus pulls shared library toward the largest category, while degrading performance on the remaining ones.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We studied behavioral credit assignment in cooperative language-model teams whose agents keep fixed parameters and act through natural-language skills. GRSE executes each question several times under the same skill libraries, compares the executions agent by agent, and attributes the teams outcome to individual agentskill pairs. Structured diagnosis grounds each attribution in checked execution steps, and the resulting credit drives targeted, validated skill updates. On HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors, GRSE outperforms MASkills on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except multi-hop, with the largest gains on multi-hop questions, where the answer depends on evidence passed between the two agents. Its gains also rest on better retrieval rather than on fewer declined answers alone. Accurate credit also makes GRSE robust: starting from library with planted harmful skills, it credits every planted skill with the correct sign and restores the score of clean library, whereas MASkills, which credits each trajectory on its own, rewards harmful skill for successes in which it is merely present and ends below its starting point. Learned libraries also transfer between HotpotQA and LoCoMo multi-hop questions without harm, and only GRSE gains further from training on the target task itself. These results suggest that comparing executions of the same task is practical way to determine which agent, and which of its behaviors, should change.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: GRSE trades training compute for more accurate credit: executing each question 𝐺=4 times raises actor-token cost by 1.62.9 over MASkills and wall-clock time by 1.31.8 (Appendix E). The overhead is confined to training, since test-time inference is unchanged. Furthermore, GRSE is defined for any number of agents, but we evaluate two-agent sequential teams on two questionanswering benchmarks with two open-weight actors and one critic model. Larger teams, non-sequential communication, longer tool-heavy tasks, and other critic models remain to be tested in the future.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: In our experiments, we use only publicly available benchmarks, HotpotQA and LoCoMo, under their respective licenses. All models are open-weight and run locally. Because GRSE writes skills in natural language, humans can inspect and edit the learned libraries for safety before deployment.

sections.title: A Experimental Details
sections.content: Models and serving. The actor is Qwen3.827B (Qwen Team, 2026) or Gemma4-31Bit (Gemma Team, 2026); Qwen3.8-27B serves as critic and optimizer in all runs. All models are served with vLLM 0.29 on two NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs each (tensor parallelism 2, context length 65,536), with thinking mode disabled. Generation is capped at 4,096 tokens for the actor, 4,000 for the critic, 1,200 for skill induction and consolidation, and 800 for refinement. The critic decodes in JSON mode with structured diagnosis that violates the citation constraints is returned once for repair. Data and checkpoints. Table 7 lists the data, their splits, and model checkpoints. Both datasets are used in their official releases, and both models are loaded from Hugging Face. LoCoMo is split by conversation, so no conversation appears in two splits. The per-category setting trains one library per question category; the mixed setting trains one library on all four categories. Category 5 (adversarial) is excluded, following MASkills and Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025). Decoding. Training rollouts use each models default sampling parameters (temperature 1.0, top-𝑝 0.95, top-𝑘 20 for Qwen and 64 for Gemma), so that rollouts of the same question can differ. On LoCoMo, validation is greedy; on HotpotQA, validation uses the training sampling parameters. All reported test scores evaluate the final (iteration5) libraries with greedy decoding. MASkills on LoCoMo follows its released per-category runner, Hyperparameters. Table 8 lists the training settings. GRSE and MASkills share every setting except the number of rollouts per question: GRSE samples 𝐺 = 4 team trajectories per question and MASkills one. Both start from empty libraries and run five iterations. For skill evolution methods, we use the mean of category-specific token F1 and the smoothed BLEU as training reward on LoCoMo to reflect both answer content and exact wording; token F1 on HotpotQA. The operator schedule Ω applies refinement and induction every iteration, consolidation every second iteration, and pruning every second (HotpotQA) or third (LoCoMo) iteration. Both methods use the same output-format handling for skill files: induced and consolidated skills are normalized to valid front matter before parsing, and skill bodies may use up to 1,200 tokens. Baselines. CoT-SC draws five samples at temperature 0.7 and returns the majority answer; Self-Refine runs at most three feedback rounds; all other prompting calls are greedy. The full-context baseline limits answers to 32 tokens.

With the empty library, the retriever greps pizza, which matches the turns around the answer but not the answer itself, tries two narrower patterns that match nothing, and returns NO_EVIDENCE, so the reasoner declines. With the final library, the retriever recognizes the matched turn as question and fetches the turns that follow it, as its learned skill adjacent-context-expansion prescribes, and the reasoner answers correctly. This question is one of the 56 declined questions that GRSE turns correct with cited evidence (5.2), and the responsible skill is retrieval procedure, the most common skill type on LoCoMo  (Table 9)  . The skill performs the same questionanswer expansion that repairs the perturbed library in Robustness Case 1 (Appendix C, Figure 5). Case B: more specific answer (Qwen3.8, HotpotQA, GRSE). On What occupation was shared by David Yates and Pietro Germi? (gold: director), the passages call Yates filmmaker who has directed films and Germi an actor, screenwriter, and director. With the empty library, Agent 1 offers Filmmaker (or director) and Agent 2 keeps the broader term (Figure 3). With the final library, Agent 1 follows the steps of two learned skills, answer-disambiguation-and-minimalism and constraint-based-entity-validation: it classifies the question as asking for an attribute, checks each persons stated roles against the passages, and keeps the role both passages support. Agent 2 answers director. This is the typical HotpotQA gain in Table 3: wrong answer becomes correct without new evidence, through more precise reading of the passages that the empty library already had.

sections.title: D Ablation Analysis
sections.content: Table 10 shows the ablation results. GRSE w/o structure removes the failure-diagnosis schema and its checks. GRSE with 𝐺=1 samples one trajectory per question, leaving the critic no in-group contrast. GRSE with the DAPO filter keeps four rollouts but, following the dynamic sampling of DAPO (Yu et al., 2025), passes only groups with differing rewards to the critic. GRSE w/ label, which we assume different tasks should have unique skills, additionally conditions the critic on the question category and groups update evidence by category.

sections.title: E Runtime Analysis
sections.content: Table 11 compares the training cost of GRSE and MASkills for the main-result runs. Token usage. GRSE executes each training question 𝐺=4 times, so its training rollouts use 3.84.3 the actor tokens of MASkills (e.g., 23.3M vs. 6.1M on LoCoMo with Qwen3.8). Validation costs about the same for both methods, which reduces the overall overhead to 1.73.0 (45.4M vs. 26.6M). Wall-clock time.
